715.title: Bhishma's boon
715.hook: Shantanu gives his son power over his own death, and why Hindus still offer water to Bhishma
715.carry: he had no child, so hindus offer him water
715.howItsDone: Some Hindus remember Bhishma on a day called Bhishma Ashtami, offering water in his name, a rite usually made for one's own ancestors, since he left no children to make it for him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one word, mother, a chariot ride to Hastinapura, and a son honoring his father's bride. Matru devo bhava: honor a mother as god.

Shantanu has just heard everything his son did at the fisherman's house: the throne given away, the lifelong vow, the bride brought home and called mother. Bhishma asked for nothing in return. He only told his father what he had done. Now his father gives him something anyway, and it's rare: a say over his own death.
screen: `THE THRONE, THE VOW, THE BRIDE.` → `HE ASKED FOR NOTHING.` → `DEATH ONLY WITH HIS LEAVE.`

segments.voice: The text says Shantanu was pleased by the hard thing his son had done. Death will not come near you while you wish to live, he tells him; it will come only with your leave. Tradition calls this icchamrityu, death at will. Look at the trade. The son gave away his future: a crown, a marriage, children of his own. The father answers with the one thing no one gets to choose, the hour of his own death. Remember it. Many years from now, lying on a bed of arrows, Bhishma will use this gift, waiting for the sun to turn north before he lets death come. But today's teaching is about the children he gave up. In Hindu tradition, the living care for the dead. Children and grandchildren offer water to their ancestors, a rite called tarpana, and food in the larger rite called shraddha. A man with no children has no one to make them. Bhishma chose that, for his father's happiness. And here's how the tradition answers him. On a day called Bhishma Ashtami, remembered as the day he finally let death come, many Hindus offer water in his name, the way they would for their own grandfather. He gave up having a family, so the whole tradition became his family. Readers still weigh the vow: some honor it as devotion to a father; some ask hard questions about a king who let his son pay that price. The Mahabharata holds both, and moves on to the bride. Her story begins long before this marriage.
screen: `ICCHAMRITYU: DEATH AT WILL.` · `HE GAVE UP CROWN, MARRIAGE, CHILDREN.` · `NO CHILDREN TO OFFER HIM WATER.` · `BHISHMA ASHTAMI.` · then, large: `HINDUS OFFER HIM WATER.`

segments.voice: In tarpana, many Hindus offer water from cupped hands, naming the people who came before them. If there's a glass of water near you, hold it. Bring to mind someone who gave something up so your life could go well: a parent, a grandparent, someone who was never really thanked. Say their name quietly, as a prayer if you pray, or simply as thanks. Then, when you can, pour a little onto a plant or the earth, the way tarpana gives water back.
Bhishma's vow. A son gave up his line for his father; his father gave him death at his own leave; and the tradition gives him the water no child could.
Your line: he had no child, so Hindus offer him water. Next, the bride's own story. See you tomorrow.

716.title: Raised by the river
716.hook: a king's daughter is raised by fishermen, and the epic's own answer to what makes a person
716.carry: conduct, not birth, shows who you are
716.howItsDone: In some Hindu rites, such as weddings, a family's gotra, the line it traces itself back to, is named aloud, so the story of where a family began is spoken at its most important moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a father's boon, death only with his son's leave, and the water Hindus still offer him. He had no child, so Hindus offer him water.

A hawk flies over the Yamuna with a leaf in its claws. On the leaf is a king's seed, sent to his queen. The king is Vasu, called Uparichara, and he was out hunting, the text says, thinking of his wife, when it fell. He caught it on a leaf and gave it to a hawk to carry home. But a second hawk sees the first, takes the bundle for meat, and attacks. In the struggle, the leaf drops into the river. This is where Satyavati's story begins.
screen: `A HAWK OVER THE YAMUNA.` → `A KING'S SEED ON A LEAF.` → `IT FALLS INTO THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the river lives a fish who is not a fish. She's Adrika, an apsara, a celestial woman, under a curse to live in that shape. She swallows what falls. Some time later, fishermen catch her, and inside they find two human children, a boy and a girl. Adrika's curse ends, and she rises back to the sky. The fishermen take the twins to the king, and the king makes a choice. He keeps the boy, who will grow up to be King Matsya. The girl he gives to the chief of the fishermen: let her be your daughter. She grows up on the river, carrying the smell of fish. Her name is Satyavati. Remember what she told Shantanu: I'm the daughter of the chief of the fishermen. Every word true. Now see where the poem takes her. This fisher girl becomes a queen of the Kurus, and the great-grandmother of the cousins the great war is about. Her first son will be Vyasa, the sage Hindus honor for arranging the Vedas and telling this very epic. Many teachers point to it: the greatest teacher in the story is a fisherwoman's son. And the epic says it outright, later on. A serpent asks Prince Yudhishthira who is truly a Brahmin. His answer: look for truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct. If those are in someone born low and missing in someone born high, birth doesn't decide it. India's history has also ranked people by birth, by caste, and that has done real harm; many Hindu saints and reformers have pushed back, pointing to stories like these.

segments.voice: In many Hindu rites, the priest asks your name and your gotra, your family line. Then add one quality you want people to find in you: truth, patience, kindness. In this epic, that counts too.

717.title: Vyasa, born on an island
717.hook: a sage, a ferry and a fragrance: the birth of Vyasa, the teacher Hindus thank on Guru Purnima
717.carry: guru purnima thanks vyasa and every teacher
717.howItsDone: Vyasa is honored as a teacher in Hindu tradition, and some Hindus keep the full moon called Guru Purnima, also known as Vyasa Purnima, as a day to thank their teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyavati, a king's daughter raised by the chief of the fishermen, and the epic's own teaching. Conduct, not birth, shows who you are.

Before the palace, there's a boat. Satyavati rows travelers across the Yamuna for her father, the chief of the fishermen. Ordinary work, on a wide river. One day a sage on a pilgrimage steps in and sits down. His name is Parashara. Out on the water, he looks at her, and he wants her. And the young woman holding the oar has to think fast, alone, in the middle of a river.
screen: `A FERRY ON THE YAMUNA.` → `A SAGE STEPS IN.` → `OUT ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The text gives Satyavati words here, and she uses them with care. There are sages on the banks, she says; they can see us. So Parashara makes a mist, and the banks disappear. Then her next worry: I'm a maiden, living under my father. What becomes of me? He answers that she'll remain a maiden, and tells her to ask something for herself. She asks for one thing: that her body, which has always carried the smell of fish, smell sweet. He grants it, and from then on, the text says, her fragrance carried far across the land. Some readers see a girl bargaining with the little power she has; some see a woman caught in a sage's power, asking what she can. The text lets her ask. On an island in the Yamuna she gives birth to a son, and before he leaves for the forest he promises her: whenever you think of me, I'll come. Hold that promise. He's called Dvaipayana, the island-born, and tradition knows him as Vyasa, the arranger. Hindus honor him as the sage who arranged the Vedas and gave the world the Mahabharata. That's why one full moon a year, in the month of Ashadha, is called Vyasa Purnima, or Guru Purnima, the teacher's full moon. On that day many Hindus thank their gurus: students bow to music and dance teachers, families visit spiritual teachers. The idea under it: what you know didn't start with you. It came down a line of teachers, and the boy born on that island stands near its head.
screen: `A MIST COMES DOWN.` · `ONE THING, FOR HERSELF.` · `A SON BORN ON AN ISLAND.` · `VYASA, THE ARRANGER.` · then, large: `GURU PURNIMA.`

segments.voice: On Guru Purnima, many Hindus bow to a teacher, with folded hands or by touching the teacher's feet. If you pray, thank God for them; if not, just say their name and thank you.

718.title: The prince with no equal
718.hook: Satyavati's proud son thinks no one is his equal, and Hindu teaching has a name for that
718.carry: ahamkara: the ego that says no equal
718.howItsDone: Many Hindus end a puja by offering the worship and its fruits back to God, some with the words 'Krishnarpanam astu', may it be an offering to Krishna; touching an elder's feet is another everyday bow of the ego.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati in the boat, and her island-born son Vyasa. Guru Purnima thanks Vyasa and every teacher.

Two warriors face each other, and they share a name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a powerful king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians. The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.
screen: `TWO WARRIORS, ONE NAME.` → `THE GANDHARVA COMES TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Satyavati has married King Shantanu on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons, Chitrangada and then Vichitravirya. Before the younger is grown, Shantanu dies. Bhishma keeps his word: he places Chitrangada on the throne and answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal. That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives, looking for this fight. They fight at Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, long and hard, and the Gandharva, with the illusions of his kind, kills the prince. Bhishma performs the funeral rites, and sets the boy Vichitravirya on the throne. The poem gives Satyavati no speech; her grief stays quiet. Now the teaching. Hindu thought has a name for what grew in Chitrangada: ahamkara, literally the I-maker. It's the voice that says, I did this, I'm the best, no one's my equal. The Bhagavad Gita, spoken later on this same field of Kurukshetra, says the one deluded by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer, when it's nature doing the work, and it lists pride and arrogance among the marks of a demonic nature. It isn't a rule against being good at things. Chitrangada really did win. The trouble was the story he told himself about it. That's why many Hindus end a puja by offering it back, some saying Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna, and why touching an elder's feet is a small, daily bow of the I.
screen: `A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FIGHT AT KURUKSHETRA.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `THE GITA ON PRIDE.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WIN BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you did well lately. Hold it and enjoy it; that's allowed. Then, the way many Hindus close a prayer, set it down: fold your hands and bow your head. If you pray, offer it to God, in your own words. If you don't, thank the people, the teachers and the luck that helped. Notice that the win is still yours, and lighter.

719.title: Amba's choice
719.hook: Bhishma carries off three princesses, the eldest says she has already chosen, and why brides still hold the garland
719.carry: the bride's garland is her choice
719.tomorrow: The vow that would not bend
719.howItsDone: In many Hindu weddings the couple exchange garlands, the jaimala or varmala, and many families say it recalls the swayamvara, where a princess placed a garland on the man she chose.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyavati lost her proud son Chitrangada, and a boy, Vichitravirya, was crowned. Ahamkara, the ego that says no equal.

Word reaches Hastinapura: the king of Kashi's three daughters will choose their husbands at a swayamvara, a self-choice, with kings gathered from everywhere. Vichitravirya is now a young man, and Bhishma has decided he should marry. So, with Satyavati's leave, Bhishma rides alone to Varanasi. He isn't going there to be chosen. He's going to take.
screen: `THREE PRINCESSES OF KASHI.` → `A SELF-CHOICE.` → `BHISHMA RIDES ALONE.`

segments.voice: The kings laugh at the old man come courting. He answers by lifting the three princesses onto his chariot. He names the ways a bride may be won, and says the wise think well of a bride taken by force. The kings take up weapons, and he defeats them all, among them Shalva, king of Saubha. Then he brings the sisters home to Satyavati, as if they were his daughters, the text says. It's a hard scene to hear today, and the text tells it plainly. Then the story turns. As the wedding is prepared, the eldest, Amba, speaks. In my heart, she tells Bhishma, I had already chosen Shalva, and he had chosen me. You know dharma. Do what's right. And the man who just won her by force stops. He asks the learned men of the court, and lets her go to Shalva. Her story isn't over; the poem comes back to her much later. The younger two marry Vichitravirya, who some years later falls ill and dies young, with no son. Now the teaching. The swayamvara was the epics' way of honoring a bride's choosing: Damayanti chose Nala at hers, and Draupadi's comes later in this poem. Amba's choice was already made, and when she named it as dharma, even the strongest man in the kingdom gave way. Hindu weddings still keep a trace of this. In the jaimala, or varmala, bride and groom place garlands on each other, and many families say it remembers the swayamvara, when a princess garlanded the one she chose.

720.title: The vow that would not bend
720.hook: with the Kuru line about to end, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow, and he will not give up truth
720.carry: satya: a word given is sacred
720.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, offerings to the ancestors are called shraddha, and some families keep the season called Pitru Paksha for them; the worry in this story is that no one will be left to make them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three princesses from Kashi, Amba let go, and a young king dead without a son. The bride's garland is her choice.

A family line is a thin thread, and Satyavati has watched hers fray to almost nothing. Her husband is gone. Both of her sons by him are gone. Two young widows grieve in the palace. The only grown man of the house is Bhishma, who swore years ago, so her sons would rule, never to take the throne and never to father children. Now she calls him in. The woman his vow made a queen is about to ask him to break it.
screen: `A HUSBAND, TWO SONS, GONE.` → `ONE MAN LEFT.` → `SHE CALLS HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Satyavati makes her case carefully, like someone who has thought about it at night. The offerings to the ancestors, the name of Shantanu, the whole house, she says, now rest on you. You know dharma. Take the throne, and raise children with your brother's widows, so the line goes on. She isn't asking lightly; in the world of the poem, a line with no sons means no one to make the offerings for the dead. But Bhishma says no. He reminds her what he swore, and why. Then he says, in effect: he could give up the three worlds, the kingdom of the gods, anything greater still, but he will not give up truth. The earth might lose its scent, water its wetness, the sun its glory, before he breaks his word. She asks once more, and he still holds. Here's the teaching. In Sanskrit, truth is satya, and Hindu tradition sets it near the heart of dharma. Many teachers put it this way: a promise is truth spoken ahead of time, so breaking it is a kind of lie. An Upanishad says it in three words, satyameva jayate, truth alone wins, and modern India took the line as its national motto. In Hindi, an unbreakable vow is still called a Bhishma pratigya, a vow like Bhishma's. But the poem is honest: the vow that made Satyavati queen now stands between her and an heir. Some readers see the picture of keeping your word at any cost; some see the first sign it will cost his family dearly. And Satyavati still has one thing she hasn't told anyone.
screen: `TAKE THE THRONE, SHE ASKS.` · `BHISHMA SAYS NO.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE UP TRUTH.` · `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.` · then, large: `A WORD GIVEN IS SACRED.`

segments.voice: Before a puja, many Hindus make a sankalpa: a stated intention, often with a little water in the palm. Hold your palm open. Make one small promise you can truly keep today: a call you'll return, a kind word you owe. Say it quietly, to God if you pray, or to yourself. Close your hand. Then keep it, today, the way Bhishma kept his.

721.title: She remembers, and he comes
721.hook: Satyavati tells Bhishma about her firstborn and calls Vyasa with a thought: why Hindus repeat God's name
721.carry: smarana: remembering god is itself devotion
721.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a mala of 108 beads for japa, repeating a name of God or a mantra once on each bead; others simply keep a name like 'Ram' going under their breath through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati asked Bhishma to break his vow, and he refused. Satya, a word given is sacred.

Bhishma has refused her, but he doesn't leave her empty-handed. He tells old stories of lines carried on in hard times, when a learned man was invited to father children for a house that had none. Find such a man, he says. And Satyavati, the text says, smiles, and her voice falters with shyness. Then the queen mother tells her stepson something she has carried since before she ever saw a palace.
screen: `FIND A LEARNED MAN.` → `SHE SMILES, AND FALTERS.` → `A SECRET FROM THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: She tells him about the boat: the sage Parashara, the mist on the Yamuna, the son born on an island. That son, she says, is Dvaipayana, the great sage people call Vyasa, and when he left he promised to come whenever she thought of him. If you agree, I'll think of him now. Bhishma agrees. Satyavati thinks of her son, and that's all it takes. Vyasa appears at once, the text says. He bows to his mother; she weeps and holds him, and tells him plainly what the house needs. Look back over the week: a vow and a boon, a baby in a fish, a boat and a fragrance, a proud son fallen, Amba's choice, Bhishma's no. And the one door left open is the one she opened herself, years ago, on a river. Now the teaching. In Hindu devotion, remembering isn't small. It has a name: smarana. When the boy Prahlada lists the ways to love God in the Bhagavata Purana, remembering comes third, right after hearing and singing. That's why so many Hindus keep a name of God going through the day: Ram, Ram while cooking, beads in the morning, Krishna's name before sleep. It's called naam smaran, remembering the name, or japa when it's counted on a mala. Many teachers say the idea isn't that God is far away and must be summoned. Remembering turns you toward the one who was near all along. Satyavati thinks, and her son comes. A devotee remembers, and the holy is there.

segments.voice: Many Hindus repeat a name of God, often on a mala of a hundred and eight beads. Choose a name that's dear to you: Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, or Om. Say it softly, once with each slow breath, for a couple of minutes. If you don't pray, choose a word you love, like shanti, peace, and do the same. When your mind wanders, that's fine; remembering again is the practice.
